references.text: God made his covenant with Abraham and promised to give him and his descendants the land of Canaan as an eternal possession.
God confirmed the covenant with Isaac and promised to give his descendants all these lands, in accordance with the oath he swore to Abraham.
God repeated the promise to Jacob to give him and his descendants the land where he was lying down.
God confirmed the covenant with Jacob and promised him the land that he had given to Abraham and Isaac.
God told Abraham that his descendants would be strangers in a land that was not theirs, but that they would later receive the land of Canaan.
Abraham described himself as a stranger and foreigner among the Hittites, which points to the patriarchs' status as immigrants in Canaan.
Jacob lived in the land where his father had been a stranger, in the land of Canaan – this refers to 'the land where they lived as strangers'.
God remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, which is the direct context for Exodus 6:4.
Abraham lived as a stranger in the promised land, in tents together with Isaac and Jacob, who were co-heirs to the same promise.
The patriarchs confessed that they were strangers and foreigners on earth, longing for a better homeland.
Stephen refers to God promising to give Abraham and his descendants the land as a possession, even though he gave him no inheritance in it.
Direct theological connection: Confirmation of the same covenant and promise of the land of Canaan given to strangers.
Thematic parallel: Historical confirmation of the same covenant-promise regarding the land of Canaan as an inheritance.
Contextual reference: Confirmation that the land given to the fathers in Exodus is the same one Jeremiah refers to.
Theological contrast: The promise to give the land (Exodus) stands in opposition to the fulfillment of the oath as scattering (Ezekiel).
Direct allusion: The psalm confirms and celebrates the same covenant promise of the land of Canaan.
Prophetic fulfillment: Confirmation that the covenantal gift of the land is tied to God's eternal relationship with His people.
Theological contrast: The promise to give the land (Exodus) stands in contrast to the possibility that the land will be laid waste (Leviticus).
